Quick Summary

The Alexiad is a historical work written by Anna Comnena, a Byzantine historian and daughter of Emperor Alexius I Comnenus. It chronicles the life and reign of her father, offering a pro-Byzantine perspective on the early Crusades. Anna, who received a comprehensive education, wrote the Alexiad while in a convent after a failed plot against her brother, Emperor John II Comnenus. 1

of her father’s reign (1081–1118), relying on various materials left by her husband, Nikephoros Bryennios (d.1138). Bryennios had received the commission from Alexios’ widow. Husband and wife were both noted intellectuals, but with very different interests—theological and philosophical for Anna, military and diplomatic for Nikephoros. The campaign narratives, which dominate the Alexiad (after the initial Komnenian coup), and associated diplomacy, originated as notes, drafts, and near-finished text inherited by Anna from Nikephoros. He used official sources to supplement his own direct knowledge. His hand is detectable through a particular style of anecdote scattered across the text. Anna was responsible for Constantinopolitan material (some political, some dealing with trials of noted intellectuals), for plugging gaps and for giving shape to the whole.

summary
The Alexiad, written in the twelfth century by a Byzantine princess, Anna Komnene, tells the story of the Byzantine Empire during the reign of her father, offering accounts of its political and military history, including its involvement with the First Crusade. Structure and Features of Anna Komnene’s Alexiad: Emergence of a Personal History introduces new methods of research for studying the Alexiad, aiming primarily at analysing Anna Komnene’s literary expression. The book’s approach focuses mainly on the author, the subject, the structure and the inner stylistic features, as well as the genre itself.
